# Overview

Robust Dissimilarity-based Principal Angle Analysis (RoDPAA) identifies
participant-level variation shared by two data views measured on the same
participants, such as the gut microbiome and the fecal metabolome of one
cohort. Each view is represented by a dissimilarity of its own, so that each
retains a geometry appropriate to its data type, for example Bray-Curtis
dissimilarity for microbial abundances and Euclidean distance for
log-transformed metabolite intensities.

For each view, RoDPAA estimates a signal subspace from the dissimilarity
matrix, measures how closely the two subspaces are aligned, tests by
permutation how many aligned directions are shared, and returns one score per
participant for each shared direction. Full details of the method are given in
the RoDPAA manuscript.

```{r setup}
library(RoDPAA)
```

# Example data

The package provides a simulated data set, `rodpaa_example`, with two views
measured on the same 80 participants, generated as
$$X_v = F_J W_v + F_{I,v} U_v + E_v, \qquad v = 1, 2,$$
where $F_J$ contains two shared factors common to both views, $F_{I,v}$ is one
additional factor of view $v$ that is independent of the other view, and $E_v$
is noise. The settings are given in `?rodpaa_example`.

```{r}
str(rodpaa_example, give.attr = FALSE)
```

The matrices `view1` (80 x 50) and `view2` (80 x 40) contain the data, with
participants in rows. The matrix `shared` contains the true shared factors $F_J$ and
is used below to assess the estimates.

# Input types

`rodpaa()` accepts each view in one of three forms, set by the argument
`input`. The default is `input = "dissimilarity"`.

| `input` | What to supply for each view | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `"dissimilarity"` (default) | An $n \times n$ dissimilarity matrix or `dist` object | Any data-appropriate dissimilarity, for example Euclidean distance, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity or other dissimilarities suited to the data |
| `"data"` | An $n \times p$ data matrix, participants in rows | Euclidean distance or Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, computed internally: select `"euclidean"` or `"bray"` for each view. For any other dissimilarity, supply the dissimilarity matrices directly with `input = "dissimilarity"` |
| `"kernel"` | An $n \times n$ symmetric similarity matrix | Advanced use, when similarity matrices are already available |

In every case, the two views must contain the same participants in the same
order, and RoDPAA uses the inputs exactly as supplied. Any preprocessing, for
example a centered log-ratio or logarithmic transformation, should therefore
be applied beforehand.

# Constructing the dissimilarities

Both example views are continuous, and Euclidean distance is used for each:

```{r}
D1 <- dist(rodpaa_example$view1)
D2 <- dist(rodpaa_example$view2)
```

The two views may use different dissimilarities. For example, for a user's own
microbial relative abundances (`microbiome`) and metabolite intensities
(`metabolome`), with participants in rows, a typical choice is

```{r, eval = FALSE}
D1 <- ecodist::distance(microbiome, method = "bray-curtis")  # Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
D2 <- dist(log(metabolome))                                  # Euclidean distance on log scale
```

# Fitting the model

RoDPAA is fitted to the two dissimilarity matrices of the simulated example
data. The main arguments are written out below with their default values: the
signal ranks are selected with the variance rule (`rank_method = "variance"`,
`var_thresh = 0.80`), which is explained in the next section, and the shared
dimension is selected by the permutation test with 1,000 permutations,
Bonferroni correction and significance level 0.05. Because the permutation
test is random, a seed is set for reproducibility.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
fit <- rodpaa(D1, D2,
              input = "dissimilarity",            # dissimilarity matrices
              rank_method = "variance",           # signal-rank rule
              var_thresh = 0.80,                  # 80% of the eigenvalue sum
              n_perm = 1000,                      # number of permutations
              alpha = 0.05,                       # significance level
              correction_method = "bonferroni")   # multiple-testing correction
fit
```

# Choosing the signal ranks

Each dissimilarity matrix is converted into a centered similarity matrix
$K_v$ by Gower double-centering. The signal rank $\hat r_v$ is the number of
leading eigenvectors of $K_v$ that form the signal subspace of view $v$. The shared dimension is tested within
these subspaces, so the signal ranks should capture the structured variation
of each view without admitting many noise directions. `rodpaa()` provides
three options:

| Situation | Setting |
|---|---|
| General use, including eigenvalues that decline gradually without a clear gap | `rank_method = "variance"` (default), with threshold `var_thresh` |
| A few large eigenvalues are clearly separated from the rest | `rank_method = "relative_diff"` (elbow) |
| The signal ranks are known from the study design or fixed in advance | `r1` and `r2` |

The variance rule keeps the smallest number of eigenvalues that account for
at least `var_thresh` (by default 80%) of the sum of the positive
eigenvalues. The elbow rule places the cut at the largest relative drop
$(\hat\lambda_{v,j} - \hat\lambda_{v,j+1}) / \hat\lambda_{v,j}$ between
consecutive positive eigenvalues. The eigenvalues are stored in
`fit$eigenvalues1` and `fit$eigenvalues2`. A scree plot of their square roots
(for Euclidean distance, the singular values of the centered data matrix)
shows which situation applies:

```{r}
scree <- function(eigenvalues, r, main, n_show = 30) {
  d <- sqrt(pmax(eigenvalues, 0))
  plot(head(d, n_show), type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 0.7, las = 1,
       xlab = "Component index", ylab = "", main = main, bty = "l")
  mtext("Square root of eigenvalue", side = 2, line = 3.3)
  abline(v = r + 0.5, lty = 2)
}
```

```{r scree-example, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 1. Scree plots of the example data: square roots of the leading eigenvalues of the similarity matrices. The dashed line marks the signal rank selected by the variance rule."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 5, 3, 1))
scree(fit$eigenvalues1, fit$dimensions$r1, "View 1", n_show = 15)
scree(fit$eigenvalues2, fit$dimensions$r2, "View 2", n_show = 15)
```

In the example data, the variance rule retains three eigenvectors per view,
whose eigenvalues account for
`r round(100 * sum(fit$eigenvalues1[1:3]) / sum(fit$eigenvalues1))`% and
`r round(100 * sum(fit$eigenvalues2[1:3]) / sum(fit$eigenvalues2))`% of the
eigenvalue sums. This agrees with the generating model (two shared factors and
one additional factor per view). The square roots of the first three
eigenvalues (the singular values) also stand clearly above the rest
(Figure 1), so the elbow rule selects the same signal ranks.

# Interpreting the output

**Shared intensities** (`fit$shared_intensities`). These are the cosines of
the principal angles between the two signal subspaces. They lie between 0 and
1, and values close to 1 indicate strong alignment. The first two are close
to 1, indicating strong alignment between the views along these directions.
The third is close to 0 and reflects view-specific variation.

**Shared dimension** (`fit$k_hat`). The permutation test identified two shared
directions. The test is summarized by `summary()`:

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

The full results are stored in `fit$permutation$table`:

```{r}
fit$permutation$table
```

The column `significant` indicates whether the adjusted P-value is below
`alpha`. The shared dimension $\hat k$ counts the leading significant
components up to the first non-significant one. A component that is
significant but follows a non-significant one is therefore not counted in
$\hat k$. The column *Shared* printed by `summary()` shows which components
are counted.

**Shared factors** (`fit$shared_factors`). An $n \times \hat k$ matrix with one
row per participant and one column per shared direction:

```{r}
head(round(fit$shared_factors, 3))
```

Because the true shared factors are known in this example, the estimates can
be assessed directly by comparing the subspace spanned by the estimated shared
factors with the subspace spanned by the true shared factors $F_J$. The
function `subspace()` of the **pracma** package returns the largest principal
angle between two subspaces, in radians, where 0 means that the subspaces
coincide:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("pracma", quietly = TRUE)}
angle <- pracma::subspace(fit$shared_factors, rodpaa_example$shared)
round(angle, 3)                  # radians
round(angle * 180 / pi, 1)       # degrees
```

The angle is small, so RoDPAA recovers the true shared subspace.

The fitted object is a list. Its components are listed by `names()`:

```{r}
names(fit)
```

The main components are:

| Component | Description |
|---|---|
| `shared_factors` | An $n \times \hat{k}$ matrix of participant-level shared factors, obtained by averaging the paired shared directions of view 1 and view 2 |
| `k_hat` | Estimated shared dimension |
| `shared_intensities` | Shared intensities (cosines of the principal angles) |
| `O_J1`, `O_J2` | Paired shared directions of view 1 and view 2 |
| `O_I1`, `O_I2` | View-specific directions |
| `eigenvalues1`, `eigenvalues2` | Eigenvalues of the two similarity matrices |
| `dimensions` | Shared dimension (`k_hat`), number of extracted directions (`k_extracted`) and signal ranks (`r1`, `r2`) |
| `permutation$table` | Shared intensity, P-value, adjusted P-value and significance of each component |

# Visualizing the results

```{r intensity, fig.cap = "Figure 2. Shared intensities. Filled points are components counted in the shared dimension; the grey band is the central 95% of the permutation null distribution."}
plot(fit)
```

In Figure 2, the first two components lie well above the permutation null
distribution, whereas the third lies within it.

```{r pvalue, fig.cap = "Figure 3. Bonferroni-adjusted permutation P-values on the negative log10 scale. The dashed line marks the significance level. Triangles mark P-values of 0, drawn at 1/B."}
plot(fit, type = "pvalue")
```

```{r scores, fig.cap = "Figure 4. Participant scores on the first two shared factors."}
plot(fit, type = "scores")
```

The shared factors can be used in downstream analyses, for example as
predictors in regression models of clinical outcomes, or as input to
clustering.

# Alternative input formats

**Data matrices.** With `input = "data"`, RoDPAA computes the dissimilarities
from the data matrices, with one dissimilarity specified per view. The result
is identical to that obtained above:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
fit_data <- rodpaa(rodpaa_example$view1, rodpaa_example$view2,
                   input = "data",
                   dissimilarity1 = "euclidean", dissimilarity2 = "euclidean",
                   verbose = FALSE)
all.equal(fit$shared_factors, fit_data$shared_factors)
```

**Similarity (kernel) matrices.** With `input = "kernel"`, the matrices must be
symmetric. They are double-centered internally, so prior centering is not
required, and they need not be positive semidefinite because only
eigenvectors with positive eigenvalues are used. The function
`dist_to_kernel()` converts a dissimilarity matrix into such a matrix:

```{r}
K1 <- dist_to_kernel(D1)
K2 <- dist_to_kernel(D2)
set.seed(1)
fit_kernel <- rodpaa(K1, K2, input = "kernel", verbose = FALSE)
all.equal(fit$shared_factors, fit_kernel$shared_factors)
```

# Exploratory directions

The argument `k_extract` sets the number of directions to extract, which may
exceed $\hat k$, for example to inspect further directions visually.
Directions beyond $\hat k$ are **exploratory**: they are not supported by the
permutation test, and the test result remains reported in `k_hat`. Here, a
third direction is extracted from the example data:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
fit3 <- rodpaa(D1, D2, k_extract = 3, verbose = FALSE)
fit3$dimensions[c("k_hat", "k_extracted")]
```

The third column of `fit3$shared_factors` is exploratory. The columns are
named `SF1`, `SF2`, ... in either case, so compare `k_extracted` with `k_hat`
before interpreting them.

# Application: ileal and rectal microbiome in the IBDMDB cohort

The data set `ibdmdb_micro` contains genus-level 16S rRNA gene counts from
paired ileal and rectal biopsies of 68 participants of the Inflammatory Bowel
Disease Multi'omics Database (IBDMDB; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019). The two biopsy
sites are treated as two views of the same participants.

```{r}
str(ibdmdb_micro[c("rectum", "ileum")], give.attr = FALSE)
```

Two representations of the microbiome profiles are used:

* **Bray-Curtis dissimilarity** on the counts.
* **Euclidean distance after the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation**,
  with a pseudocount of 1:
  $\mathrm{CLR}(x)_g = \log(x_g + 1) - \frac{1}{p}\sum_{m=1}^{p} \log(x_m + 1)$.

The rectum is used as view 1 and the ileum as view 2. The signal ranks are
selected with the default variance rule.

```{r}
d <- ibdmdb_micro

# Bray-Curtis on the counts
set.seed(1)
fit_bc <- rodpaa(d$rectum, d$ileum, input = "data",
                 dissimilarity1 = "bray", dissimilarity2 = "bray")
fit_bc

# CLR transformation, then Euclidean distance
clr <- function(X) {
  L <- log(X + 1)
  L - rowMeans(L)
}
set.seed(1)
fit_eu <- rodpaa(clr(d$rectum), clr(d$ileum), input = "data",
                 dissimilarity1 = "euclidean", dissimilarity2 = "euclidean")
fit_eu
```

Both representations identify shared structure between the two sites:
`r fit_bc$k_hat` shared directions under Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and
`r fit_eu$k_hat` under CLR-Euclidean distance.

```{r ibdmdb-intensity, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = "Figure 5. Shared intensities of the IBDMDB ileal and rectal microbiome under Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (left) and CLR-Euclidean distance (right)."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit_bc, main = "Bray-Curtis")
plot(fit_eu, main = "CLR-Euclidean")
```
